note:
A shelf of commonly taken supplements, so somebody can tick off what they already take (Kevin, 29 Aug): "The supplements should be like any other library, just a big list of commonly taken supplements that can be adjusted by bottle/dose size, with the reorder tracking and stuff… Just let me select my supplements. It could be smart enough to have some education as to what each supplement does and suggest when it should be taken."

THIS IS A TRACKER, NOT A SHOP. The first version of this file put a `careful` warning on every item including vitamin D, and a test that REQUIRED one — Kevin, same day: "putting a careful label on vitamin D is dumb. All of these stupid precautions are unnecessary. We are not selling or recommending supplements. We are making it easy for someone to track what they take within their daily routine… you need a warning that you put too many warnings on stuff." He is right, and the warnings were doing the opposite of their job: a caution on all eight is a caution on none, and it read as liability boilerplate on a screen whose only job is to let you tick off what is already in your cupboard.

So what stays is what changes how you take the thing — with food, on an empty stomach, with a full glass of water — and that lives in the how-to, where you read it while doing it, not in a warning box. What goes is everything a person did not come here for.

Brand names appear nowhere: a brand is where you buy a substance, which is a different fact.

items.name: Magnesium glycinate
items.why: The form of magnesium least likely to send you to the bathroom, which is why it is the one people take at night.

fields.tool: Check the label for ELEMENTAL magnesium — a 500 mg capsule of magnesium glycinate is not 500 mg of magnesium, it is closer to 70.
fields.release: Evening, with or without food. Splitting it across the day sits easier than taking it all at once.

items.name: Vitamin D3 with K2
items.why: The one worth having an actual blood level for — a 25-hydroxy test tells you the dose, which no label can.

fields.release: With the fattiest meal of the day. It is fat-soluble and absorption roughly doubles with food.

items.name: Creatine monohydrate
items.why: Cheap, boring, and among the very few that does what the label says. Monohydrate is the studied form; the expensive ones are not better.

fields.release: Any time of day — the muscle store fills over weeks, so consistency matters far more than timing.
fields.notice: A couple of pounds on the scale in the first fortnight is water drawn into muscle.

items.name: Omega-3 (EPA and DHA)
items.why: Read the back of the bottle, not the front — "1000 mg fish oil" is often 300 mg of the part that does anything.

fields.release: With a meal. Freezing the softgels stops the fishy repeat.
fields.notice: If it smells strongly fishy through the bottle it has oxidised.

items.name: L-glutamine
items.why: Genuinely the preferred fuel of intestinal cells. Whether supplementing it does anything for an ordinary gut is a much bigger claim than the mechanism supports.

fields.release: Empty stomach, usually first thing. It dissolves far better in hot liquid than cold.

items.name: Electrolytes
items.why: For heat, hard sweat, illness or a long fast. Not a daily requirement for most people, whatever the packaging implies.

fields.release: During or after whatever lost you the water.

items.name: Psyllium husk
items.why: Unfashionable, cheap, and it works — an unusual combination on this shelf.

fields.tool: A full large glass of water, every time. It thickens within a minute, so drink it rather than sipping at it.
fields.release: Start at half a dose and build over a fortnight — going straight to a full one is how people decide fibre does not agree with them. Keep it a couple of hours clear of medication, which it slows down.

items.name: Zinc
items.why: One of the few where taking it on an empty stomach is reliably unpleasant, and where more is clearly not better.

fields.release: With food — fasted zinc causes nausea in most people. Keep it away from iron and calcium, which compete with it for the same transport.

items.name: Vitamin B12
items.why: Worth it if you eat little or no animal food, or take metformin or long-term acid blockers. Otherwise usually already covered.

fields.release: Morning — it is mildly stimulating for some people. A sublingual lozenge is held under the tongue rather than swallowed.

items.name: Vitamin C
items.why: Absorption drops steeply above about 500 mg at a time, so a large single dose mostly ends up in the toilet. Split it if you take more.

fields.release: With food, split across the day if the dose is large.

items.name: Collagen peptides
items.why: Digested into ordinary amino acids like any other protein, so the idea that it travels to your joints is not how it works. The tendon and skin trials are small but not nothing.

fields.release: Any time. Dissolves in hot or cold without changing the taste of much.

items.name: Probiotic
items.typicalDose: per label — strain matters more than the CFU count
items.why: Effects are strain-specific, so "a probiotic" is not a thing that works or does not — the one on the label is. Most benefits stop when you stop.

fields.release: Usually away from a meal, though the label for your particular strain outranks that.
